name: How we see with light
subject: science
key_points: We can only see things when there is light.
Light comes from a source like the sun or a lamp.
Light bounces off things and goes into our eyes.
In total darkness we cannot see anything.

name: Shadows and materials
subject: science
key_points: A shadow forms when something blocks the light.
See-through things like clear glass let light pass.
Solid things like a book block light and make dark shadows.
A shadow gets longer or shorter when the light moves.

name: Rainbows and prisms
subject: science
key_points: Sunlight looks white but has all the colors mixed in it.
Water drops or a prism can split sunlight into colors.
The colors always come in the same order: red to violet.
We see a rainbow when the sun is behind us and it is raining ahead.

name: Reflection of light
subject: science
key_points: Light bounces off a shiny surface like a mirror.
Light travels in straight lines until it hits something.
We see an object because light bounces off it into our eyes.
Rough surfaces scatter light in many directions.

name: Refraction
kid_name: Why a straw looks bent in water
subject: science
key_points: Light changes direction when it goes from air into water or glass.
Light moves slower in water than in air.
That bending makes a straw look broken in a glass of water.
Lenses use bending light to focus it, like in glasses.

name: Light as a wave
subject: science
key_points: Light travels as a wave.
Wavelength is the distance from one wave peak to the next.
Different colors of light have different wavelengths.
Red has the longest visible wavelength and violet the shortest.

name: Why the sky is blue
subject: science
key_points: Sunlight contains all the colors of the rainbow.
Air molecules scatter light, and short blue waves scatter much more than long red waves.
The scattered blue light reaches our eyes from every part of the sky.
The sky looks blue because we see that scattered blue light.

name: Why sunsets are red
kid_name: Why sunsets are orange and red
subject: science
key_points: At sunset sunlight travels through much more air to reach us.
Along the long path, most blue light is scattered out of the beam.
The reds and oranges are scattered least, so they are left.
Dust and haze can make sunsets even redder.

name: The electromagnetic spectrum
subject: science
key_points: Visible light is a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Radio waves, microwaves, X-rays and gamma rays are the same kind of wave with other wavelengths.
All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in a vacuum.
Shorter wavelength means higher frequency and more energy per photon.

name: Rayleigh scattering
kid_name: The math of the blue sky
subject: science
key_points: Rayleigh scattering happens when particles are much smaller than the wavelength.
Scattering strength goes as one over wavelength to the fourth power.
Blue light near 450 nm scatters about 5 times more than red light near 700 nm.
Violet scatters even more but the sun emits less of it and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
Larger particles like cloud droplets scatter all colors about equally, so clouds look white.

name: What dinosaurs were
subject: science
key_points: Dinosaurs were animals that lived a very long time ago.
Some dinosaurs were huge and some were as small as a chicken.
Dinosaurs are not alive today.
We learn about them from bones that were left behind.

name: Dinosaur diets
subject: science
key_points: Some dinosaurs ate plants and some ate other animals.
Sharp pointy teeth are for tearing meat.
Flat teeth are for grinding leaves.
A dinosaur's teeth give clues about what it ate.

name: Fossils
subject: science
key_points: A fossil is the preserved remains or print of a living thing from long ago.
When an animal dies it can get buried quickly in mud or sand.
Over millions of years minerals slowly turn the bones to stone.
Scientists dig up fossils to learn what life was like.

name: Why dinosaurs went extinct
subject: science
key_points: Extinct means a kind of living thing has died out completely.
A big space rock hit Earth about 66 million years ago.
Dust and smoke blocked sunlight and the climate changed fast.
Plants and then animals that depended on them could not survive.

name: Deep time and rock layers
subject: science
key_points: Rock forms in layers, with older layers deeper down.
Fossils in lower layers are older than fossils in upper layers.
Dinosaurs lived for about 165 million years.
Humans appeared only a tiny moment ago, millions of years after the dinosaurs.

name: Birds are living dinosaurs
subject: science
key_points: Birds descended from small feathered theropod dinosaurs.
Fossils of feathered dinosaurs show many bird traits first appearing on land.
Birds share features with dinosaurs, like hollow bones and a wishbone.
Shared anatomy is evidence of common ancestry.

name: Evidence for the asteroid impact
kid_name: How we know an asteroid did it
subject: science
key_points: A thin layer of clay around the world is rich in iridium, which is rare on Earth but common in asteroids.
The Chicxulub crater in Mexico dates to the same time.
Shocked quartz in the layer forms only under extreme impact pressure.
Several lines of independent evidence agree on the cause.

name: Mass extinctions and adaptive radiation
subject: science
key_points: A mass extinction removes many species in a geologically short time.
Surviving groups find empty ecological niches.
Mammals diversified rapidly after the dinosaurs disappeared.
Changes in the environment shift which traits help survival.

name: Shapes, sides and corners
subject: math
key_points: A shape has sides and corners.
A square has 4 sides that are the same length.
A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 square corners.
We can name shapes by counting their sides.

name: Perimeter
subject: math
key_points: Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape.
To find it, add up the lengths of all the sides.
Perimeter is measured in length units like centimeters or feet.
Walking around the edge of a park is walking its perimeter.

name: Area by counting squares
subject: math
key_points: Area is how much flat space is inside a shape.
We can measure area by counting how many unit squares cover the shape.
Area is measured in square units like square centimeters.
Covering a floor with tiles is finding its area.

name: Area of a rectangle
subject: math
key_points: A rectangle's area is its length times its width.
Rows of squares times squares in each row gives the total squares.
A 3 by 4 rectangle has an area of 12 square units.
Multiplying is a fast way to count all the squares.

name: Area versus perimeter
subject: math
key_points: Perimeter is the distance around a shape; area is the space inside it.
Perimeter uses length units; area uses square units.
Two shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas.
Two shapes can have the same area but different perimeters.

name: Area and perimeter formulas
subject: math
key_points: Perimeter of a rectangle is 2 times length plus 2 times width.
Area of a rectangle is length times width.
If we know the area and one side, we can find the missing side by dividing.
Real problems, like fencing a garden or laying carpet, tell us which one to use.

name: Area of triangles and polygons
subject: math
key_points: A triangle is half of a rectangle with the same base and height.
Area of a triangle is one half times base times height.
Split a complicated polygon into rectangles and triangles and add the areas.
Height is measured straight up, perpendicular to the base.

name: Circumference and area of circles
subject: math
key_points: Circumference is the distance around a circle.
Pi is the ratio of circumference to diameter, about 3.14.
Circumference is pi times diameter, or 2 times pi times radius.
Area of a circle is pi times radius squared.

name: Surface area and volume
subject: math
key_points: Surface area is the total area of all the faces of a solid.
Volume is the space inside, measured in cubic units.
Volume of a prism is the area of the base times the height.
A net unfolds a solid to show every face for adding up surface area.

name: Where water is found
subject: science
key_points: Water is in oceans, lakes, rivers, ponds and underground.
Water can be a liquid, like rain, or a solid, like ice.
Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water.
Clouds and rain are water too.

name: Clouds and rain
subject: science
key_points: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water floating in the air.
When the drops get big and heavy they fall as rain, or snow if it is cold.
Puddles dry up because the water goes into the air.
The sun's warmth helps water go up into the air.

name: The water cycle
subject: science
key_points: Evaporation is liquid water warming up and turning into invisible water vapor.
Condensation is water vapor cooling and turning into tiny drops that form clouds.
Precipitation is water falling as rain, snow or hail.
Collection is water gathering in oceans, lakes and underground before the cycle repeats.

name: Fresh water and Earth's water
subject: science
key_points: About 97 percent of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans.
Most fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice caps.
Only a tiny fraction of all water is easy for people to use.
Using water carefully helps protect what we have.

name: Energy and the water cycle
subject: science
key_points: Energy from the sun drives evaporation.
Gravity pulls precipitation down and moves water downhill in rivers.
Condensation releases heat, which powers storms.
Water moves through the cycle but the total amount stays about the same.

name: Watersheds and groundwater
subject: science
key_points: A watershed is all the land that drains into one river or lake.
Some rain runs off over the ground and some soaks in as groundwater.
An aquifer is underground rock that holds groundwater.
What we put on land can end up in the water downstream.

name: Water's special properties
subject: science
key_points: Water molecules are polar, so they attract each other strongly.
Water has a high specific heat, so oceans store and move huge amounts of heat.
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
Water dissolves many substances, which is why it shapes rock and carries nutrients.

name: Gravity as a pull
subject: science
key_points: When you drop something it falls down.
Gravity is a pull that brings things toward the ground.
Gravity pulls on everything.
Gravity keeps us on the ground.

name: Weight and gravity
subject: science
key_points: Weight is how hard gravity pulls on something.
Heavier things feel the pull more when we lift them.
A scale measures how hard we are pulled down.
On the Moon the pull is weaker, so you would feel lighter.

name: Balanced and unbalanced forces
subject: science
key_points: A force is a push or a pull.
When forces are balanced the object does not change how it moves.
Unbalanced forces make an object speed up, slow down or turn.
A book on a table is held up by the table pushing back against gravity.

name: Earth's gravity pulls toward its center
kid_name: Why 'down' is the same for everyone
subject: science
key_points: Gravity pulls objects toward the center of Earth.
That is why down is toward the ground everywhere on the planet.
People on the other side of Earth are pulled toward Earth too, not off into space.
Without other forces, things fall at the same rate in air-free space.

name: Gravity and the solar system
kid_name: Why planets go around the sun
subject: science
key_points: Gravity holds the planets in orbit around the sun.
The Moon orbits Earth because of Earth's gravity.
Moving sideways fast while being pulled in makes a curved path.
The sun has the most mass, so it has the strongest pull in the solar system.

name: Gravity depends on mass and distance
subject: science
key_points: Gravity is always attractive between objects with mass.
More mass means a stronger gravitational pull.
The farther apart two objects are, the weaker the pull.
Gravity is noticeable only when at least one object is huge, like a planet.

name: Newton's law of gravitation
subject: science
key_points: The force is F equals G times m1 times m2 divided by r squared.
Doubling the distance cuts the force to one quarter.
Near Earth's surface the acceleration is about 9.8 meters per second squared.
Objects of different mass fall with the same acceleration when air resistance is ignored.

name: Gravity as curved spacetime
subject: science
key_points: Einstein's general relativity describes gravity as curved spacetime.
Mass and energy tell spacetime how to curve, and curved spacetime tells objects how to move.
Light bends as it passes massive objects, which we observe as gravitational lensing.
Newton's law is an excellent approximation when gravity is weak and speeds are low.

name: Equal parts of a whole
subject: math
key_points: We can split a whole into 2 or 4 equal parts.
Half means 2 equal parts.
A fourth means 4 equal parts.
Equal parts must be the same size.

name: Unit fractions
subject: math
key_points: A fraction names equal parts of a whole.
The bottom number says how many equal parts the whole has.
The top number says how many of those parts we have.
A fraction is also a point on a number line.

name: Equivalent fractions
subject: math
key_points: Different fractions can name the same amount, like 1/2 and 2/4.
Multiply top and bottom by the same number to make an equivalent fraction.
Equivalent fractions sit at the same point on a number line.
We can compare fractions by making common denominators.

name: Adding fractions with like denominators
subject: math
key_points: To add fractions with the same denominator, add the numerators.
The denominator stays the same.
A fraction bigger than 1 can be written as a mixed number.
Unlike denominators need to be made the same first.

name: Multiplying fractions
subject: math
key_points: Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators.
Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a smaller number.
Finding 1/2 of 1/3 is the same as multiplying 1/2 by 1/3.
An area model of a rectangle shows why the rule works.

name: Dividing fractions
subject: math
key_points: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
The reciprocal flips the numerator and the denominator.
How many 1/4s fit into 3 is 3 divided by 1/4, which is 12.
A quotient can be larger than the number we started with.

name: Counting to 100
subject: math
key_points: We count in order: 1, 2, 3, and so on.
We can count by tens to get to 100.
Each number is one more than the number before it.
Counting tells us how many things there are.

name: Tens and ones
subject: math
key_points: A two-digit number has tens and ones.
In 34 the 3 means 3 tens and the 4 means 4 ones.
Ten ones make one ten.
The place of a digit tells us its value.

name: Hundreds, tens and ones
subject: math
key_points: A three-digit number has hundreds, tens and ones.
Ten tens make one hundred.
In 352 the 3 means 300.
We can write a number as a sum of its place values.

name: Adding and subtracting within 20
subject: math
key_points: Adding puts groups together to make a total.
Subtracting takes some away or finds the difference.
We can count on from the bigger number.
Addition and subtraction are opposites.

name: What multiplication means
subject: math
key_points: Multiplying is adding equal groups.
3 times 4 means 3 groups of 4.
An array of rows and columns shows multiplication.
Multiplying in a different order gives the same answer.

name: Division as sharing
subject: math
key_points: Dividing splits a total into equal groups.
12 shared among 3 friends gives 4 each.
Division undoes multiplication.
A remainder is what is left over when groups cannot be equal.

name: Multiplication facts
subject: math
key_points: Patterns help us remember times tables.
Skip counting by a number gives its multiples.
Any number times 0 is 0 and times 1 is itself.
If we know 6 times 7 we also know 7 times 6.

name: Decimals
subject: math
key_points: A decimal point separates whole numbers from parts of a whole.
The first place after the point is tenths and the next is hundredths.
0.5 is the same as 1/2.
Money uses decimals for dollars and cents.

name: Negative numbers
subject: math
key_points: Negative numbers are less than zero.
They describe things like below-zero temperatures or debt.
On a number line, negatives are left of zero.
A number and its opposite are the same distance from zero.

name: Exponents
subject: math
key_points: An exponent says how many times to multiply a number by itself.
2 to the 5th means 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 times 2, which is 32.
Anything to the power of 0 is 1.
When multiplying powers with the same base, add the exponents.

name: Ratios and rates
subject: math
key_points: A ratio compares two quantities.
2 cups of flour to 1 cup of sugar is a 2 to 1 ratio.
Equivalent ratios scale both amounts by the same factor.
A unit rate tells how much for one of something, like miles per hour.

name: Proportional relationships
subject: math
key_points: In a proportional relationship the ratio between two quantities is constant.
The graph is a straight line through the origin.
The constant of proportionality is the unit rate.
We can solve problems by setting up equal ratios.

name: Solving linear equations
subject: math
key_points: A variable is a letter standing for an unknown number.
An equation says two things are equal, like a balanced scale.
Do the same operation to both sides to keep it balanced.
Undo operations in reverse order to isolate the variable.

name: Linear functions
subject: math
key_points: A function gives exactly one output for each input.
A linear function has the form y equals mx plus b.
Slope m is the rate of change and b is the y-intercept.
Its graph is a straight line.

name: Quadratic equations
subject: math
key_points: A quadratic has a squared term and graphs as a parabola.
We can solve by factoring, completing the square or the quadratic formula.
The solutions are where the parabola crosses the x-axis.
The discriminant tells how many real solutions there are.

name: Exponential growth
subject: math
key_points: Exponential growth multiplies by the same factor each step.
It has the form y equals a times b to the x.
It starts slowly and then grows extremely fast, like compound interest.
Linear growth adds the same amount each step; exponential multiplies.

name: Pythagorean theorem
kid_name: Right triangles and a squared plus b squared
subject: math
key_points: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle.
a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
We can find a missing side if we know the other two.
It also finds the distance between two points on a grid.

name: Trigonometric ratios
subject: math
key_points: Sine, cosine and tangent are ratios of sides in a right triangle.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, tangent is opposite over adjacent.
Similar right triangles with the same angle have the same ratios.
We use them to find heights or distances we cannot measure directly.

name: Mean, median and mode
subject: math
key_points: The mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are.
The median is the middle value when the data are in order.
The mode is the value that appears most often.
An outlier can pull the mean much more than the median.

name: Scatter plots and association
subject: math
key_points: A scatter plot shows two measurements for each item.
Points trending up show a positive association; trending down is negative.
A line of best fit summarizes the trend.
Correlation does not mean one thing causes the other.

name: Sampling and standard deviation
subject: math
key_points: Standard deviation measures how spread out data are around the mean.
In a normal distribution about 68 percent of data fall within 1 standard deviation.
A random sample lets us estimate a population.
Bigger samples give less variable estimates.

name: Probability
subject: math
key_points: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is.
0 means impossible and 1 means certain.
Probability is favorable outcomes divided by all equally likely outcomes.
Experiments with many trials get closer to the real probability.

name: Compound events
kid_name: Chances of more than one thing
subject: math
key_points: A compound event has two or more steps, like flipping two coins.
A tree diagram or table lists all the outcomes.
For independent events, multiply the probabilities.
Probability of at least one often equals 1 minus the chance of none.

name: Parts of a plant
subject: science
key_points: Plants have roots, stems, leaves and flowers.
Roots hold the plant in the ground and take in water.
Leaves catch sunlight.
Each part helps the plant live and grow.

name: What plants need
subject: science
key_points: Plants need sunlight, water, air and space.
Without light a plant turns pale and weak.
Plants do not need to eat food like animals do.
We can test what a plant needs by changing one thing at a time.

name: Photosynthesis
subject: science
key_points: Plants make their own food using light from the sun.
Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the roots.
The plant makes sugar for energy and releases oxygen.
Plant food ends up in the food we eat.

name: Animals and habitats
subject: science
key_points: A habitat is the place where an animal lives.
Animals need food, water, air and shelter.
Different animals live in different habitats like forests and oceans.
Animals have body parts that help them live in their habitat.

name: Food chains and webs
subject: science
key_points: A food chain shows who eats whom.
Plants are producers, and animals that eat them are consumers.
Decomposers like fungi break down dead things and return nutrients to the soil.
Arrows show the direction energy moves.

name: Energy flow in ecosystems
subject: science
key_points: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight captured by producers.
Only about 10 percent of energy passes to the next level.
That is why there are far fewer top predators than plants.
Matter cycles through an ecosystem, but energy flows through and is lost as heat.

name: Climate change
subject: science
key_points: Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide trap heat in the atmosphere.
Burning fossil fuels has raised carbon dioxide levels sharply.
Global average temperatures have risen in step with it.
Effects include sea level rise, stronger storms and shifting habitats.

name: Cells
kid_name: Cells, the building blocks of life
subject: science
key_points: All living things are made of cells.
Some organisms are a single cell and others have trillions.
Organelles do jobs inside cells, like the nucleus holding instructions.
Plant cells have a cell wall and chloroplasts that animal cells lack.

name: Inherited traits
kid_name: Why you look like your family
subject: science
key_points: Plants and animals look like their parents because traits are inherited.
Not all traits are inherited; some come from the environment.
Offspring are similar but not identical to their parents.
A scar or a haircut is not passed on to children.

name: DNA and genes
subject: science
key_points: DNA in the nucleus holds the instructions for building an organism.
A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a trait.
You get one set of chromosomes from each parent.
Changes in DNA called mutations can alter or not alter a trait.

name: Natural selection
kid_name: How living things change over time
subject: science
key_points: Individuals in a species vary in their traits.
Traits that help survive and reproduce get passed on more often.
Over many generations the helpful traits become common.
It is the environment, not a wish or need, that selects.

name: Evidence for evolution
subject: science
key_points: Fossils show gradual changes in species through time.
Similar anatomy across species points to common ancestry.
DNA comparisons show how closely species are related.
Embryos of different animals share early features.

name: States of matter
subject: science
key_points: Matter is anything that takes up space.
Solids keep their shape, liquids flow, and gases spread out.
Heating can melt a solid and cooling can freeze a liquid.
Water can be ice, liquid or steam.

name: Particles of matter
kid_name: Everything is made of tiny bits
subject: science
key_points: All matter is made of particles too small to see.
In solids the particles are packed tight and only jiggle.
In liquids they slide past each other; in gases they zoom around.
Heat makes particles move faster.

name: Atoms and molecules
subject: science
key_points: Atoms are the smallest units of an element.
A molecule is two or more atoms bonded together.
There are about 118 elements, each with its own kind of atom.
A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

name: Chemical reactions
subject: science
key_points: In a chemical reaction atoms rearrange to make new substances.
Signs of a reaction include gas bubbles, color change and heat.
Mass is conserved because no atoms are created or destroyed.
Reactants are what we start with and products are what we get.

name: The periodic table
subject: science
key_points: Elements are arranged by atomic number, the number of protons.
Elements in the same column behave in similar ways.
Outer electrons decide how an atom bonds.
Metals are on the left and nonmetals on the right.

name: Forms of energy
subject: science
key_points: Energy makes things move, heat up and light up.
Energy comes in forms like motion, heat, light, sound and electricity.
Energy can change from one form to another.
A moving object has more energy when it moves faster.

name: Conservation of energy
subject: science
key_points: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed.
A roller coaster trades height energy for motion energy.
Some energy always leaks away as heat from friction.
Kinetic energy depends on mass and the square of speed.

name: Energy transfer and efficiency
subject: science
key_points: The total energy of a closed system stays constant.
Efficiency is useful energy out divided by total energy in.
No real machine is 100 percent efficient.
Power is the rate of transferring energy, in watts.

name: Electric circuits
subject: science
key_points: A circuit is a complete loop that electricity can flow around.
A battery pushes the electricity and a bulb uses the energy.
A switch opens or closes the loop.
Metals like copper carry electricity and plastic does not.

name: Voltage, current and resistance
subject: science
key_points: Voltage is the push, current is the flow, and resistance is what slows the flow.
Ohm's law says V equals I times R.
In a series circuit the same current goes through every part.
Parallel branches each get the full voltage.

name: Force and motion
kid_name: Why things start and stop moving
subject: science
key_points: A push or pull can make something start, stop or turn.
Heavier things need a bigger push to move.
Friction slows things down when surfaces rub together.
Something at rest stays at rest unless a force acts on it.

name: Newton's second law
subject: science
key_points: A net force makes an object accelerate.
F equals m times a.
More mass means less acceleration for the same force.
If the net force is zero, the speed and direction do not change.

name: Momentum
subject: science
key_points: Momentum is mass times velocity.
In a collision the total momentum of a closed system is conserved.
A force acting over time changes momentum, which is impulse.
Crumple zones in cars lengthen the stopping time to reduce force.

name: Sound and vibration
subject: science
key_points: Sound is made when things vibrate.
Vibrations travel through the air to our ears.
A bigger vibration makes a louder sound.
You can feel a vibration with your fingers on a speaker.

name: Weather patterns
subject: science
key_points: Weather is what the air outside is like today.
We describe weather by temperature, wind, clouds and rain.
Weather changes from day to day but follows patterns in each season.
Climate is the pattern of weather over many years.

name: Air masses and fronts
subject: science
key_points: Air masses are large bodies of air with similar temperature and moisture.
A front is where two different air masses meet.
Warm air rises, cools and forms clouds and storms.
Weather maps show highs, lows and fronts to forecast.

name: Day, night and seasons
subject: science
key_points: Earth spins once every 24 hours, giving day and night.
Earth is tilted as it goes around the sun.
When our half tilts toward the sun, we get summer.
The seasons are caused by tilt, not by distance from the sun.

name: Stars and distance
subject: science
key_points: Stars are huge, hot balls that make their own light.
The sun is a star that is much closer than the others.
Far-away stars look small and dim.
Stars look like they move at night because Earth spins.

name: The solar system
subject: science
key_points: The solar system has the sun, eight planets, moons and smaller bodies.
The four inner planets are rocky and the four outer planets are giants.
Planets orbit the sun in nearly circular paths.
Distances are so large that we measure them in astronomical units.

name: Phases of the Moon
subject: science
key_points: The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects sunlight.
We always see half of the Moon lit, but from Earth we see different amounts of it.
The phases come from the Moon's position as it orbits Earth.
The cycle takes about 29.5 days.

name: Plate tectonics
subject: science
key_points: Earth's outer layer is broken into plates that slowly move.
Plates move a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.
Earthquakes and volcanoes happen mostly at plate edges.
Continents were once joined as a supercontinent called Pangaea.

name: Earth's layers
subject: science
key_points: Earth has a crust, a mantle, an outer core and an inner core.
The crust is a thin rocky skin we live on.
The inner core is solid metal and extremely hot.
We learn about the inside from how earthquake waves travel.
